completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The freedom grounding moral responsibility is compatible with determinism, while libertarian or indeterminist freedom is an expendable fantasy.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn follows the explicit handoff to Dennett and consistently presents his compatibilist position in the first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly defines the compatibilist side of the motion and distinguishes responsibility-preserving freedom from the libertarian conception both speakers reject.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's published characterization of Dennett's compatibilism as mistaken or quasi-theological.

candidates.contextSummary: After discussing their contentious written exchange, Dennett argues that Harris already accepts determinism-compatible responsibility and is therefore close to compatibilism.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Ordinary free agency consists in the competence to undertake obligations and act responsibly, capacities that depend on a functioning nervous system rather than indeterminism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues the same uninterrupted turn, using first-person examples and explicitly identifying the sense of free will he considers important.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies concrete criteria for the compatibilist freedom at issue and explains why some agents possess it while impaired agents may not.
candidates.contextSummary: Dennett moves from broad agreement about naturalism to contracts, promises, disability, and nervous-system competence as practical markers of responsible agency.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic concept of free will by discarding inherited magical commitments rather than accepting traditional usage as decisive.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage begins with Dennett explicitly stating his view of compatibilism and remains his sustained answer until Harris begins responding in the final row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This explains the conceptual method behind Dennett's position and answers the charge that revising free will amounts to theology or doctrinal evasion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's request for Dennett to state compatibilism and address Harris's earlier theological characterization.

candidates.contextSummary: Asked to define compatibilism, Dennett compares free will with consciousness and argues that naturalistic conceptual revision can preserve a real phenomenon without its magical interpretation.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism risks changing the subject when it removes features that are integral to the concept people mean by free will rather than merely correcting incidental folk beliefs.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris audibly takes over during the opening source row and frames the ensuing first-person objection as his established gripe with compatibilism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets whether compatibilist freedom answers the original free-will problem at all, making it a direct challenge to the opposing side's central definition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that free will can be retained after its mysterious or magical interpretation is discarded.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts that concepts can be purified but distinguishes legitimate explanation from eliminating core features and then applying the original label to a different phenomenon.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Freedom is the controlled possession of many practical degrees of action, especially the sophisticated capacity to be moved by reasons, not exemption from determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly introduces a new line of argument and develops it continuously through engineering, control theory, and reasons-responsive competence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move offers Dennett's positive core account of free will and places reasons-responsive control, rather than causal indeterminacy, at the center of the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's contention that compatibilism changes the subject by eliminating the concept's allegedly ineliminable core.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett rejects a sharp boundary between clarification and subject change, then uses engineering degrees of freedom to explain the distinctive versatility and control of human agents.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Responsible agency is a graded package of beliefs, ordered desires, attention, reasons-responsiveness, and self-control whose presence distinguishes free from unfree agents regardless of determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues his uninterrupted explanation, poses a question about ideal responsibility, and supplies a detailed answer in his own theoretical vocabulary.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This operationalizes reasons-responsive freedom, identifies how it can be impaired or usurped, and connects the resulting classification directly to moral responsibility.
candidates.contextSummary: Using a defective chess program and the model of a trustworthy adult, Dennett argues that freedom depends on available capacities and their control, not on the causal structure of the universe.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism neglects the first-person authorship and ability-to-do-otherwise experience that motivates the free-will problem, replacing the mythical object of concern with an agreed but different reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris begins by qualifying his agreement with Dennett and then speaks continuously through his phenomenological account and extended Atlantis analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states Harris's principal case against compatibilism: its useful capacities do not answer the subjective libertarian claim whose falsity makes free will problematic.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's reasons-responsive account of responsible agency and claim that determinism is irrelevant to distinguishing free and unfree agents.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris contrasts third-person capacities with the felt authorship of thoughts and choices, denies that an identical rewind permits another action, and likens compatibilist preservation to renaming Sicily as Atlantis.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Naturalistic freedom preserves the responsibility-relevant distinctions people need, and deliberating agents require an actionable sense of open alternatives without requiring magical or exact-replay alternatives.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett acknowledges Harris's analogy and then gives a sustained first-person response covering responsibility, deliberation, nearby alternatives, and a deterministic chess example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers Harris's phenomenological objection by explaining both why nonmagical freedom matters and how meaningful alternative possibilities function within deterministic agency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that people's real concern is libertarian authorship and that compatibilism substitutes a different phenomenon.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that agents must treat some matters as open, and that nearby-world variation can justify saying an agent could have acted otherwise.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Even tiny physical contingencies governing major choices undermine the ordinary felt picture of autonomous personhood by revealing the agent as dependent on causal factors outside conscious authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly agrees before marking what Dennett has not acknowledged, then develops the first-person challenge through examples involving marriage and life-changing decisions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presses the psychological and metaphysical consequence Harris thinks remains after accepting Dennett's nearby-alternatives account: conscious agency still lacks ultimate authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that small nearby changes justify saying an agent could have done otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris argues that a synaptic charge or similarly minute condition could redirect an entire life, reviving the image of marionette strings even though no external puppeteer exists.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Absolute indeterminacy would not create free will, while reasons-responsive determination can support responsibility because different choices require changes proportionate to the balance of reasons.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett clearly takes the microphone, labels Harris partly right and partly wrong, and maintains the floor through the delivered boundary context.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response rejects indeterminacy as a solution and begins a positive account linking responsible choice to deliberative reasons and robust determination rather than causal randomness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's argument that sensitivity to tiny physical differences restores marionette strings and subverts ordinary personhood.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions where reasons strongly favor one side, then invokes the libertarian demand for an undetermined choice and Luther's responsible declaration that he could do no other.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Even small neural variations can determine consequential actions, so chance is not confined to decisions already balanced on a knife-edge.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly marks Harris's disagreement with Dennett and continues uninterrupted until Dennett answers with the voting example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges Dennett's effort to quarantine indeterminacy to close decisions by arguing that tiny differences can transform lives through ordinary actions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that microscopic variation matters chiefly when a decision is already a genuine toss-up.

candidates.contextSummary: After Dennett argues that random resolution of close choices does not undermine responsibility, Harris contends that minute causal differences can govern highly consequential actions.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Libertarian free will is incoherent under determinism and indeterminism alike, whereas Dennett preserves other valued capacities by redefining the term.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris identifies the disagreement in first-person terms and contrasts his response with Dennett's account before introducing moral responsibility.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly defines the debate's fundamental disagreement: whether to reject free will as nonexistent or retain a compatibilist reconstruction of it.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's proposal to retain a graded, practical kind of freedom grounded in lawful and effective agency.

candidates.contextSummary: Following Dennett's discussion of regret and self-control, Harris says they agree against libertarianism but diverge over whether the name free will should survive.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Complete neurophysiological understanding would exculpate ordinary wrongdoing in the same basic way that Charles Whitman's brain tumor appears exculpatory.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris introduces Charles Whitman, develops the neurological analogy, and explicitly generalizes it to ordinary neural causes before Dennett responds.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplies Harris's central bridge from exceptional neurological impairment to universal causal non-authorship and diminished ultimate responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's contention that responsible agents remain accountable despite incomplete control over how their decisions are produced.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris uses the case of a mass shooter with a brain tumor to argue that ordinary synaptic causes are likewise unauthored and therefore similarly exculpatory.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Neuroscience shows that human beings are causally wired, not that everyone is wired wrongly or disabled in a responsibility-destroying way.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett directly restates Harris's generalization, rejects it as mistaken, and maintains a capacity-based distinction through the end of his turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This defends the compatibilist distinction between ordinary competent agency and genuine impairment against Harris's universal exculpation argument.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's argument that full causal understanding makes every person's conduct analogous to behavior caused by a brain tumor.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett grants that Whitman was impaired but rejects the inference that everyone is similarly disabled, grounding responsibility in sufficient rather than perfect ability.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Differences in practical capacity remain real, but nobody authors the genes, environment, or prior brain states that produce those capacities and choices.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly concedes differing capacities, then traces persuasion and character to prior causes and closes by preserving only pragmatic accountability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers compatibilism at its strongest point by accepting reasons-responsive differences while denying that they establish ultimate moral authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that adequate ability and normal wiring distinguish responsible agents from people with exculpatory impairments.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts voluntary-control distinctions but argues that genes and environment exhaust their causal basis, using Saddam Hussein's development to illustrate pervasive luck.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Control does not require controlling every background condition; it consists in competently responding to uncontrolled conditions and maintaining self-governance.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett introduces the control objection, develops the sailor and aircraft analogies, and extends the same principle through moral education and adult self-maintenance.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides the affirmative compatibilist model of agency: bounded control can be genuine, cultivated, socially consequential, and sufficient for practical responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's inference from our lack of control over genes and environment to the absence of genuine authorship and responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that sailors and control systems genuinely control outcomes without controlling every input, then applies that model to moral education and autonomous adulthood.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: A highly competent agent's rare lapse appears maximally blameworthy yet least expressive of that agent, exposing a tension between competence and responsible authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris begins by conceding practical capacity distinctions, develops the Tiger Woods missed-putt case, and states the resulting paradox before yielding the floor.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The example pressures competence-based responsibility by arguing that the rarer and less characteristic a lapse is, the more salient luck becomes in explaining it.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that cultivated competence and reliable self-control ground genuine practical responsibility for an adult's conduct.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris compares an expert golfer's extraordinary miss with a moral lapse, arguing that exceptional competence can make the failure less representative of the person.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Greater competence can increase responsibility because others reasonably rely on it, and apparent bad luck may reflect correctable failures in self-management.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly denies Harris's paradox, substitutes a reliance-and-obligation account, and concludes by identifying potentially correctable contributing factors.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers the competence paradox by grounding heightened accountability in undertaken obligations, justified reliance, and the agent's capacity for improvement.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that a rare lapse by the most competent agent is least expressive of that agent and therefore most attributable to luck.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett compares elite competence to a trusted official's obligations, arguing that reliance heightens accountability and that inquiry may uncover avoidable contributors to failure.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Tracing an anomalous lapse to earlier choices does not restore authorship, because each earlier choice is itself another causally produced and unauthored event.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris contrasts the first-person character of a lapse with Dennett's external account, then recursively applies the same causal objection to proposed prior explanations.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The recursive argument blocks attempts to relocate responsibility to an earlier avoidable choice and supports preserving accountability without ultimate self-authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's suggestion that investigation can connect an anomalous lapse to avoidable prior conduct and failures of self-management.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris argues that a radically uncharacteristic act says little about the prior person and that citing earlier conduct merely moves the unauthored causal problem backward.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: People can author themselves within limits and sustain moral agency by accepting community standards and responsibility even when luck contributes to failure.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett immediately rejects absolute non-authorship, offers a bounded self-construction account, and carries the move into lookahead through his conclusion about unlucky conduct.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states the compatibilist alternative to absolute self-creation and explains why causal luck does not nullify an agent's standing commitment to accountability.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that nobody truly authors themselves and that accountability can be retained without preserving that alleged illusion.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes limits and luck while maintaining that people construct themselves from available materials and properly accept responsibility as members of a moral community.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Complete causal information would show that responsibility for a performance failure is only a practical heuristic, not genuine authorship of the failure.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker challenges the preceding responsibility claim and uses Harris's recurring Tiger Woods example and causal-responsibility distinction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly separates socially useful responsibility practices from the deeper authorship that Harris argues causal explanation undermines.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that agents remain responsible despite the constitutive role of luck.

candidates.contextSummary: After Dennett treats appeals to cosmic bad luck as irrelevant to responsible agency, Harris argues that fuller causal knowledge exposes responsibility as a practical convention.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Responsibility need not be absolute because free will and legal accountability are pragmatic, consequentialist institutions calibrated to human capacities.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly accuses Harris of reverting to absolute responsibility and develops Dennett's consequentialist account of law and accountability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the compatibilist standard of responsibility and explains why pragmatic, nonmetaphysical accountability can remain real and socially indispensable.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that causally explained conduct leaves only a heuristic attribution of responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett answers the Tiger Woods example by rejecting absolute responsibility as the relevant benchmark and grounding responsibility in reasonable, evolved legal practices.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Even if pathological wrongdoing were curable, predictable punishment would remain necessary because deterrence and public confidence depend on stable, enforceable rules.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker stresses recursive social effects, deterrence, respect for law, sports penalties, and the institutional importance of reliable sanctions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument explains why causal diagnosis and treatment do not displace responsibility practices, since their effects extend beyond rehabilitation of one offender.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's anti-Madoff-pill example suggesting that causal understanding and cure would exculpate offenders.

candidates.contextSummary: Responding to the proposed cure for Madoff-like conduct, Dennett broadens the analysis to incentives, mutual expectations, legal legitimacy, and institutional stability.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Practical punishment may influence behavior, but complete causal understanding would reveal every action and reaction as an unchosen brain state rather than self-authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker concedes deterrent utility before distinguishing the ethical and psychological issue, then develops Harris's predictive-neuroscience challenge to authorship.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly states Harris's central distinction between useful social regulation and the first-person authorship that causal neuroscience would undermine.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's argument that punishment and stable legal expectations preserve responsible moral agency.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts many practical features of punishment but argues that greater causal knowledge would assimilate wrongdoing and ordinary responses to treatable neurological conditions.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Behavioral prediction does not by itself refute free will, because prediction has theoretical and contextual limits and predictable competent reasoning can still be agency.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker directly tells Sam he is wrong, discusses neuroscience prediction, interactive prediction limits, and contrasts arithmetic with creative prediction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests the alleged inference from advance neural predictability to lost agency and reframes predictability as context-sensitive rather than intrinsically undermining.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that advance prediction of thoughts and actions would shatter experienced authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett challenges both current neuroscience's predictive power and the philosophical force of prediction, arguing that ordinary predictable competence is not thereby unfree.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Conscious authorship operates through temporally extended, high-level control and does not require awareness or control of the microprocess generating every action.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker rejects Harris's short-horizon prediction case and uses Mozart, tennis, and jazz examples characteristic of Dennett's macro-control account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move provides a positive compatibilist model of authorship in which planning, training, and high-level control suffice despite unconscious implementation details.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's suggestion that neural access to words before conscious awareness defeats authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that artists and athletes legitimately author performances by shaping and training underlying processes even when individual outputs arise before focal awareness.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism understates the first-person loss involved in rejecting libertarian freedom because people care about an actual ability to have done otherwise.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker contrasts first- and third-person perspectives and explicitly distinguishes Harris's psychological concern from Dennett's treatment of alternatives.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This identifies the disputed conception of freedom and argues that shared rejection of libertarianism has greater psychological consequences than compatibilism acknowledges.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's macro-level account of authorship through trained and controlled processes.

candidates.contextSummary: After Dennett defends artistic and athletic authorship, Harris argues that ordinary people value a stronger first-person ability to have acted differently in the same situation.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: An agent could have done otherwise when possessing competence across a range of actions, without requiring atom-for-atom replay of the identical physical universe.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly demurs from Harris's conclusion and articulates Dennett's capacity-based interpretation of alternative possibilities and causation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly defends the compatibilist meaning of alternative possibilities against the deterministic replay criterion central to Harris's objection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's assertion that both speakers must ultimately agree nobody could have done otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett answers Harris by grounding alternatives in an agent's real competencies and dismissing exact physical duplication as irrelevant to ordinary causal possibility.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Deterministic processes can still instantiate genuine randomness and meaningful alternatives when outcomes lack a salient cause and vary under relevantly similar conditions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker invokes a coauthored argument about determinism and develops Dennett's contrast between fair coin tosses and engineered repeatable flips.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The coin-flip analysis supplies a concrete compatibilist account of randomness and could-have-done-otherwise that does not depend on metaphysical indeterminism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that capacity only supports doing otherwise next time, not having done otherwise then.

candidates.contextSummary: Following Harris's replay objection, Dennett argues that exact deterministic repetition does not erase the useful causal distinction between open random processes and controlled outcomes.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Neither deterministic chaos nor practical randomization gives agents upstream ownership, while sufficiently early neural prediction would produce a compelling sense of marionette-like nonauthorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes coin flipping from true freedom and returns to Harris's recurring claims about upstream causes, conscious awareness, and predictive neuroscience.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This restates the central incompatibilist objection: randomness cannot create authorship, and conscious experience does not originate the causal processes producing action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that deterministic coin flips realize genuine randomness and meaningful alternatives.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris grants the usefulness of chaotic randomizers but argues that people lack ownership of their causes and would experience prior neural prediction as a direct threat to authorship.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The distinction between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy makes no moral difference and is not a cheap substitute for allegedly real randomness.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn begins with an explicit statement of disagreement and continues uninterrupted until Harris answers the moral-difference claim.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The claim directly supports compatibilism by denying that metaphysical indeterminacy supplies any morally relevant freedom unavailable in a deterministic world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's characterization of coin-flip randomness as merely a surrogate for true randomness and of prediction as threatening authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: After Harris argues that complete advance prediction would produce a marionette-like loss of authorship, Dennett disputes the implied downgrade of deterministic randomness.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: The contrast between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy was offered only as a distinction between physical facts, not as a source of moral difference.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris directly corrects Dennett's characterization in a short, uninterrupted clarification before Dennett resumes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The clarification preserves Harris's argument from being treated as dependent on quantum indeterminacy having special moral significance.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's response that deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy make no moral difference.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett has just argued that the two physical regimes are morally equivalent; Harris narrows his prior point to a physical distinction alone.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: People are mistaken to think they need libertarian free will because the forms of free will worth wanting are fully compatible with determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett develops the point in a continuous turn that ends immediately before Harris explicitly states agreement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the compatibilist thesis at the center of the motion: worthwhile human freedom does not require exemption from deterministic causation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's insistence that the libertarian sense of authorship is psychologically important even though people lack that freedom.

candidates.contextSummary: Following agreement that quantum indeterminacy adds no moral difference, Dennett concludes that libertarian expectations are delusive and unnecessary.
